title: Trust Functions: Near Lossless Weak-to-Strong Generalization by Learning to Trust the Weak Teacher
claim: Filtering weak supervision with a learned trust score, applied iteratively through a chain of students, nearly matches ground-truth training and compounds gains.
layout: 3 panels: pipeline top-left, chain bottom-left, two result plots right; robot icons
description: The left side shows two stacked method diagrams that read left to right. The top diagram, 'Learning to Trust (L2T)', starts with green-outlined Labeled Data feeding a neural trust function (NTF) drawn as a network. Red-outlined Unlabeled Data goes through a cartoon Weak Teacher robot to produce Weak Labels. The NTF and a purple Filter box produce yellow-outlined High Trust Data, which trains a Strong Student robot. A blue rounded box encloses the L2T core. Solid arrows mean train and dashed arrows mean inference. The bottom diagram, 'Weak-to-Strong Chain', passes the Weak Teacher through two blue L2T boxes. This produces a Strong Student and then a larger, armored Stronger Student. Labeled data loops back into each L2T box. The right side has a bar chart comparing NTF with ground truth on MCQA, Math and Chess, and a line chart where the NTF Chain pulls ahead of plain NTF as student size grows from 4B to 14B.
caption: (1) Learning to Trust (top-left): Given a small labeled set, we train a neural trust function (NTF) to predict whether weak labels are reliable. We then use the NTF to filter weak labels to produce a high-trust subset, which is used to train the strong student model. (2) Weak-to-Strong Chain (bottom-left): This procedure can be applied iteratively across multiple generations of students, forming a weak-to-strong chain that compounds gains and outperforms direct weak-to-strong transfer as students scale. (3) Results (right): Across multiple domains, L2T achieves near-lossless performance compared to training on ground-truth (GT) labels (top). Moreover, chaining yields snowballing gains across the iterations (bottom).
abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization studies how to improve a strong student using supervision from a weaker teacher when reliable labels are scarce. We view this primarily as a data selection problem, where the key challenge is to identify which weak labels are reliable enough to serve as a training signal. To address this, we introduce trust functions that assign each weak label a scalar trust score and use these scores to filter weak supervision. Across several domains, including world knowledge, quantitative reasoning, and strategy games, trust filtering yields students that match and sometimes surpass ground-truth supervision, achieving near-lossless weak-to-strong generalization. Moreover, trust functions enable an iterative weak-to-strong chain that compounds gains by training a student and reusing it as the next teacher, amplifying the gains. There are several mechanisms to which advantage of trust functions can be attributed.
